Title: My beef with AI credit pricing
Author: Elena Verna
Source: https://www.elenaverna.com/p/i-hate-ai-credits-pricing
Date: Nov 14, 2025

With new technology comes new pricing models, but the one we’re all using right now is AI Credits.
Using LLMs is expensive and each usage costs real money.
Companies use credits to make sure that usage doesn’t spike out of control and bankrupt them, but credits create problems.
Reason #1: Customer doesn’t know the price up front.
You have no idea how much each action costs; lack of predictability deters customers and ties to fairness.
Reason #2: Prices don’t feel fair.
Perception of how many credits an action should cost differs from actual compute cost; customers learn in retrospect and feel taken advantage of.
Reason #3: There’s no apples-to-apples comparison.
Each company defines credits differently and doesn’t share definitions.
Some map credits to tokens 1:1, some 1:10, some 1:1000, others have “slow” unlimited tiers.
Credits become a made-up metric, so customers can’t compare value across vendors.
Reason #4: Customer Support becomes impossible.
Support teams get flooded by customers trying to forecast plan costs or complaining about usage value, which makes the role harder.
Reason #5: Companies will exploit this confusion.
Because credits are arbitrary, vendors can make credits cost more or charge more credits per action to increase revenue.
Elena notes she hasn’t seen this at Lovable; they aim to make actions 20–30% cheaper by optimizing prompts and efficiency.
Outlook.
Credits are a necessary evil while LLM costs are high.
As costs drop toward ~50% profitability, companies will revert to measurable, transparent models (per-user or concrete units).
Vendors that stick rigidly to credits will lose; customers will churn due to price unpredictability and fake metrics.

Tokens and Transparency
Brief: Goal: explain how teams can use tokens or usage as a transparent meter without letting it dominate pricing.
Audience: product and finance leads shaping hybrid usage models.
Promise: give examples of transparent usage meters paired with predictable anchors.
Source inspiration: management piece from Lovable referencing tokenized meters; cite Elena Verna, “I hate AI credits pricing.” REVIEW: add full citation and date.
Problem: Teams like the clarity of metered billing, but pure pay-per-use makes revenue volatile and buyers nervous about surprise bills.
Product teams need a transparent meter without forcing customers to live entirely on tokens.
Stakes: Without a predictable anchor, finance leaders block deals because spend is hard to forecast.
If usage meters are hidden or unclear, customers assume the vendor is gaming the bill.
Over-indexing on flat plans starves heavy users and removes the incentive to optimize efficiency.

Alternatives that mix predictability and tokens:
- Baseline subscription plus metered overages: keep a platform fee or seat minimum, then charge tokens for variable-heavy features.
Works when there is a clear floor of value each month.
- Prepaid usage blocks: sell token packs that roll over or expire quarterly, paired with a light base fee.
Helps procurement budget an envelope while keeping usage variable.
- Tiered pools with visibility: buckets of included tokens per tier, with real-time balance shown in-app.
Customers understand what is included and when they will pay more.
- Commit-to-consume: annual commitment priced on expected token use, reconciled quarterly.
Buyers get a discount for predictability; vendor protects revenue.
- Efficiency incentives: lower token burn for optimized workflows or off-peak usage.
Encourages behavior that benefits both sides without hiding the meter.

Proof and examples:
- Developer platforms often blend seats for collaboration with per-unit execution charges.
REVIEW: add concrete examples and ranges.
- Data vendors sell flat data access plus per-query compute to keep heavy users honest.
REVIEW: cite a public pricing page.
- Messaging APIs combine monthly minimums with per-message rates, signaling the meter while keeping invoices steady.
REVIEW: add reference link.
Action: Choose a visible meter (tokens, requests, compute time) and expose it in-product.
Anchor revenue with a base fee or minimum commit, then graduate usage when value scales.
Publish the meter math in FAQs and invoices; let customers self-forecast before purchase.
Track burn rates by customer segment to adjust pools, discounts, and efficiency incentives.

Snippets:
- Hybrid billing lands best with a base subscription that guarantees a revenue floor while tokens meter variable-heavy features; finance teams can forecast, and customers still see how usage drives cost.
- Prepaid token packs paired with a light platform fee give procurement a clear budget envelope while keeping room for spiky workloads; rollover or quarterly expiry signals how much runway is left.
- Commit-to-consume plans price tokens against expected use for the year, then true up quarterly; buyers get discounts for predictability while the vendor locks in baseline revenue.
- Transparency checklist: expose the meter unit in-product, show real-time balance or burn, publish the math on invoices, and let buyers self-forecast before they commit.
- Lower token burn for optimized workflows or off-peak usage lets vendors reward efficiency without hiding the meter, keeping buyers engaged instead of feeling punished by growth.
